questions.question: What are the three layers of Snowflake's architecture?
options: Database storage, query processing (compute) and cloud services
questions.explanation: Snowflake separates storage, virtual-warehouse compute and the cloud services layer that handles auth, metadata and optimization.

questions.question: What happens when a warehouse created with AUTO_SUSPEND=60 sits idle for a minute?
options: It scales down to the smallest size
It suspends and stops consuming credits
It keeps running at half the credit rate
questions.explanation: AUTO_SUSPEND is measured in seconds. A suspended warehouse uses no credits, and AUTO_RESUME restarts it on the next query.

questions.question: Why can two users query the same table from two differently sized warehouses without contention?
options: Compute is separate from storage, so each warehouse reads the same data independently
Snowflake copies the table into each warehouse
Queries are queued and run one at a time
The larger warehouse locks the table first
questions.explanation: Warehouses are independent compute clusters over shared storage, so workloads don't compete for the same resources.

questions.question: Which object sits directly inside a database in Snowflake's object hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Organization → account → database → schema → tables, views and other objects. Warehouses are account-level compute, not database objects.

questions.question: What is SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA?
options: A copy of your production data for testing
A read-only shared database with TPC-H and TPC-DS sample schemas
A schema created automatically by COPY INTO
questions.explanation: It's a share from Snowflake with benchmark sample data, so every account can practice without loading anything.

questions.question: Which is the top-level system-defined role in an account?
questions.explanation: ACCOUNTADMIN encapsulates SYSADMIN and SECURITYADMIN, so it should be granted to very few users and used sparingly.

questions.question: Why grant a custom role like data_engineer to SYSADMIN?
options: So SYSADMIN inherits its privileges and can manage the objects it creates
Because custom roles can't be granted to users
It is required before any table can be created
questions.explanation: Rolling custom roles up into SYSADMIN keeps the hierarchy intact, so administrators can manage every object those roles own.

questions.question: What does GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA ... do?
options: Grants SELECT only on tables that exist today
Schedules the grant for a future date
Automatically grants SELECT on tables created in that schema later
questions.explanation: Future grants apply to objects created after the grant, so new tables are readable without another GRANT.

questions.question: A masking policy returns '***MASKED***' unless CURRENT_ROLE() is DATA_ENGINEER. What does data_analyst see when querying the column?
questions.explanation: Masking policies are evaluated at query time for the querying role. The stored data itself never changes.

questions.question: Why does tag-based masking scale better than attaching masking policies table by table?
options: A policy attached to a tag protects every column carrying that tag, across tables
Tags encrypt the data at rest
Tags remove the need for roles
questions.explanation: Tag a column as PII once and the tag's masking policy follows it, instead of maintaining policies on every table.

questions.question: Which query reads a table as it was 60 seconds ago?
questions.explanation: AT(OFFSET => -60) uses Time Travel to read the table state 60 seconds in the past.

questions.question: What is true of a zero-copy clone right after it is created?
options: It shares micro-partitions with the source and only stores data that changes later
It duplicates all of the source's storage immediately
It is a live view that mirrors every later source change
It can only clone single tables
questions.explanation: Clones are copy-on-write: they start as metadata pointing at the same micro-partitions and diverge only as either side changes.

questions.question: Who can recover data that has moved into Fail-safe?
options: Any user with the UNDROP privilege
The table owner with AT queries
Nobody, because Fail-safe is metadata only
Snowflake Support, as a last resort
questions.explanation: Fail-safe is a non-configurable 7-day period after Time Travel for permanent tables, and recovery goes through Snowflake Support.

questions.question: What does LATERAL FLATTEN(input => raw:line_items) return?
options: The JSON as a single string
One row per element of the line_items array
A count of the line items
questions.explanation: FLATTEN explodes an array or object into rows, exposing each element through the VALUE column.

questions.question: When is adding a manual clustering key a bad idea?
options: When the table has a VARIANT column
When the table is small, because reclustering costs credits without improving pruning
questions.explanation: Clustering keys pay off on very large tables with selective filters. On small tables, automatic clustering maintenance just spends credits.

questions.question: What does the PUT command do?
options: Uploads local files to an internal stage
Loads staged files into a table
questions.explanation: PUT runs from a client such as the Snowflake CLI and uploads files to an internal stage. COPY INTO then loads them.

questions.question: Why does running the same COPY INTO twice load zero rows the second time?
options: COPY INTO deletes the files after loading them
The table is locked after the first load
The file format rejects duplicate rows
Load metadata records which files were already loaded
questions.explanation: Table load metadata is kept for 64 days, so COPY INTO skips files it already loaded unless you set FORCE=TRUE.

questions.question: Which option best fits an application emitting individual events continuously with low latency?
questions.explanation: Snowpipe Streaming writes rows through an API without staging files, which suits continuous event producers.

questions.question: What triggers an auto-ingest Snowpipe on an external stage?
options: Cloud storage event notifications when new files land
A stream on the target table
questions.explanation: With AUTO_INGEST=TRUE, cloud event notifications (such as S3 events) tell Snowpipe that new files have arrived.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of an external table?
options: The data stays in cloud storage, so queries are typically slower than on loaded tables
It can't be queried with SQL
questions.explanation: External tables avoid loading, but reading files in place usually can't match the performance of native micro-partitioned tables.

questions.question: How does a standard stream represent an UPDATE to a row?
options: As a DELETE and an INSERT, both with METADATA$ISUPDATE = TRUE
questions.explanation: Streams record updates as a DELETE of the old values plus an INSERT of the new ones, flagged with METADATA$ISUPDATE.

questions.question: What does WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('products_stream') add to a task?
options: It creates the stream if it's missing
It skips the scheduled run when the stream has no new changes
It runs the task whenever the stream is queried
questions.explanation: The WHEN condition is checked before the run, so the task skips runs with nothing to process.

questions.question: In a task graph, what does AFTER do?
options: Delays the task by a set amount of time
Runs the task after the warehouse suspends
Makes the task run once its predecessor finishes
questions.explanation: AFTER declares a predecessor, turning standalone tasks into a DAG with a single root.

questions.question: What does TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes' mean for a dynamic table?
options: Its content should be no more than about 5 minutes behind its sources
It keeps 5 minutes of Time Travel
questions.explanation: Target lag is a freshness goal. Snowflake schedules refreshes to keep the table within that lag of its sources.

questions.question: Why might a team choose Dynamic Tables over Streams and Tasks?
options: They support arbitrary procedural logic and external calls
They let you declare the result while Snowflake manages refreshes and dependency order
questions.explanation: Dynamic Tables are declarative: you write the SELECT and set a lag, and Snowflake handles incremental refresh and ordering.

questions.question: Where does a Snowpark DataFrame transformation execute?
options: Inside Snowflake's engine, pushed down as SQL
questions.explanation: Snowpark builds a query plan lazily and executes it in Snowflake when an action such as collect() or save_as_table() runs.

questions.question: What does QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1 keep?
options: The latest row for each order_id
The whole table sorted by date
questions.explanation: QUALIFY filters on the window function result, keeping the top-ranked row in each partition.

questions.question: Which layer holds business-level aggregates such as revenue by category?
questions.explanation: Bronze holds raw data, Silver cleaned and conformed data, and Gold business-ready aggregates.

questions.question: When is a Python UDF a better choice than plain SQL?
options: For loading files from a stage
For logic SQL can't express easily, such as custom text cleaning
questions.explanation: UDFs extend SQL with Python logic while still running inside Snowflake.

questions.question: What does APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT trade for speed?
options: Exactness, because it returns an estimate
questions.explanation: It uses HyperLogLog to estimate distinct counts with a small error, much faster than COUNT(DISTINCT ...) on large data.

questions.question: What is a serverless task?
options: A task whose compute Snowflake manages, created without a WAREHOUSE
A task that runs outside Snowflake
A task that can't be monitored
questions.explanation: Serverless tasks use Snowflake-managed compute that is sized automatically from recent runs.

questions.question: Which query shows recent task runs and their errors?
questions.explanation: TASK_HISTORY returns task runs with their state, scheduled time and error details.

questions.question: What do dbt Projects on Snowflake remove the need for?
options: An external orchestrator or separate dbt runtime
questions.explanation: dbt Core runs natively inside Snowflake, developed in Workspaces and deployed as a Snowflake object.

questions.question: What is a Snowsight Workspace used for in this program?
options: Git-backed editing and running of the dbt project inside Snowsight
questions.explanation: Workspaces connect to a Git repository so you can edit, run and deploy the dbt project without leaving Snowsight.

questions.question: Why deploy the dbt project as a Snowflake object instead of only running it interactively?
options: So it can run on a schedule or from the Snowflake CLI
It removes the need for a warehouse
questions.explanation: A deployed project is a governed object that tasks or the CLI can execute repeatedly.

questions.question: What does a Git repository object in Snowflake let you do?
options: Push commits from SQL worksheets only
Fetch and read a remote repo's files from SQL, such as LIST @my_repo/branches/main
questions.explanation: It keeps a synced clone of the remote so Snowflake can list and execute files from specific branches.

questions.question: What makes a migration script idempotent?
options: It can only ever run once
Running it again leaves the same end state, for example with CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS
It has a version number in its name
questions.explanation: Idempotent DDL can be re-run safely, which matters when pipelines retry or replay scripts.

questions.question: Where should Snowflake credentials for a GitHub Actions workflow live?
questions.explanation: Secrets are encrypted and injected at runtime, and never belong in the repository itself.

questions.question: In the workflow you built, when does the prod deploy run?
options: On every push to any branch
questions.explanation: Feature branches deploy to dev, and only reviewed changes merged to main promote to prod.

questions.question: Why run the same versioned scripts against dev and prod?
options: Because prod can't run SQL directly
So both environments end up with identical objects from source control
So dev can be deleted afterwards
questions.explanation: Deploying the same source-controlled scripts everywhere prevents environments from drifting apart.

questions.question: Which Query Profile signal suggests a warehouse is too small for a large sort?
options: Bytes spilled to local or remote storage
questions.explanation: Spilling means intermediate results didn't fit in memory, so the query overflowed to disk, which slows it down.

questions.question: When is the result cache reused?
options: For identical query text when the underlying data hasn't changed
For any query on the same table
questions.explanation: Persisted results are reused for the same query text as long as the data hasn't changed and the query is deterministic.

questions.question: What does resizing a warehouse from XSMALL to SMALL require?
options: Just an ALTER WAREHOUSE statement, with no downtime
questions.explanation: Resizing takes effect for new queries without downtime. Queries already running finish on the old size.

questions.question: Which scaling policy favors keeping running clusters fully loaded to save credits?
questions.explanation: Economy starts extra clusters only when there's enough sustained load, while Standard prioritizes low queuing.

questions.question: What can a Resource Monitor do when usage reaches 100% of its credit quota?
options: Suspend the warehouses assigned to it
questions.explanation: Triggers can NOTIFY, SUSPEND (after running queries finish) or SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE (cancelling running queries).

questions.question: What backs a Snowsight dashboard tile?
questions.explanation: Each tile is created from a saved worksheet query and its chart settings.

questions.question: Where does a Streamlit in Snowflake app run?
options: Inside Snowflake, with no external hosting
On a separate server you deploy
questions.explanation: Streamlit in Snowflake hosts the app natively, using Snowflake compute and governance.

questions.question: What does a Cortex Analyst semantic model describe?
options: Tables, columns, synonyms and verified queries so an LLM can write accurate SQL
questions.explanation: The semantic model maps business vocabulary to your physical tables so generated SQL targets the right objects.

questions.question: Why add verified queries to a semantic model?
options: They give Cortex Analyst known-correct SQL for common questions, improving accuracy
questions.explanation: Verified queries act as trusted examples that ground the SQL generated for similar questions.

questions.question: Why are Cortex Analyst answers governed?
options: It copies data out of Snowflake first
The generated SQL runs under the user's role, so RBAC and masking policies still apply
questions.explanation: Cortex Analyst generates SQL, but that SQL executes with the caller's privileges like any other query.

questions.question: What do Snowpark ML Modeling estimators share with scikit-learn?
options: They only run on your laptop
The same fit and predict interface
questions.explanation: Snowpark ML wraps familiar scikit-learn-style APIs while executing the work on Snowflake compute.

questions.question: What do built-in ML Functions like FORECAST let you do?
options: Get forecasts or anomaly flags from SQL without building a model yourself
Train deep neural networks by hand
questions.explanation: ML Functions package common ML tasks behind SQL, so analysts can use them without writing model code.

questions.question: Why preprocess with Snowpark ML transformers instead of to_pandas()?
options: The work runs on Snowflake compute and scales without pulling data locally
questions.explanation: to_pandas() moves all the data into client memory, while Snowpark ML transformers push the work down.

questions.question: What compute can a Snowflake Notebook run on?
options: A virtual warehouse or Container Runtime
questions.explanation: Notebooks run on a warehouse, or on Container Runtime for workloads that need packages or GPUs.

questions.question: Which is a governance benefit of training models inside Snowflake?
options: Data never leaves the platform, so existing access controls still apply
It removes the need for roles
questions.explanation: Keeping training in-platform avoids uncontrolled data copies and keeps RBAC and masking in force.

questions.question: What does a Feature Store Entity define?
options: The join key or keys features are looked up by, such as customer_id
questions.explanation: Entities describe the keys that connect feature views to training data and inference requests.

questions.question: What does point-in-time correctness prevent?
options: Label leakage from feature values recorded after each label's timestamp
questions.explanation: Joining features as of the label time stops the model from learning information it wouldn't have had at prediction time.

questions.question: Why log-scale a skewed revenue column?
options: To turn it into a categorical feature
To reduce the influence of extreme values
questions.explanation: A log transform compresses long tails so a few very large values don't dominate the model.

questions.question: What does refresh_freq='1 day' on a FeatureView do?
options: Keeps the feature data refreshed daily
Deletes the view after a day
Limits queries to once a day
questions.explanation: Managed feature views are refreshed on their schedule so features stay current.

questions.question: Which of these is a time-based feature?
options: Days since a customer's first order
questions.explanation: Recency and tenure features capture how behavior changes over time.

questions.question: What does GridSearchCV do?
options: Samples a few random hyperparameter combinations
Tries every combination of the listed hyperparameters and keeps the best
questions.explanation: GridSearchCV is exhaustive. RandomizedSearchCV samples combinations instead, which is cheaper for large grids.

questions.question: Which metric fits an imbalanced churn classifier better than accuracy?
questions.explanation: With few positive cases, accuracy can look high while missing churners. F1 and AUC reflect performance on the minority class.

questions.question: Why set a default version or alias in the Model Registry?
options: It is required before logging a model
Consumers call the current champion without hard-coding a version
questions.explanation: Promoting a new version becomes a registry change instead of a code change in every consumer.

questions.question: What is batch inference?
options: Scoring a whole table of rows at once
Scoring one request in real time
questions.explanation: Batch inference scores many rows in one job, typically writing the predictions to a table.

questions.question: Which signal suggests model drift?
options: Live prediction distributions moving away from training-time distributions
questions.explanation: When the data or predictions shift away from what the model was trained on, its accuracy usually degrades.

questions.question: What does Cortex Search provide?
options: Managed hybrid vector and keyword retrieval over a table
questions.explanation: Cortex Search indexes text from a table and serves low-latency hybrid search for RAG applications.

questions.question: What is the correct order of a RAG chain?
options: Retrieve relevant chunks, augment the prompt, then generate
questions.explanation: Retrieval supplies grounded context, the prompt is augmented with it, and the LLM generates the answer.

questions.question: What does AI_CLASSIFY do?
options: Sorts text or images into categories you provide
questions.explanation: AI_CLASSIFY assigns inputs to one or more labels you supply, directly from SQL.

questions.question: Why check retrieved chunks before building generation on top of them?
options: If retrieval is off, answers will be wrong or hallucinated no matter the prompt
questions.explanation: Generation quality is capped by retrieval quality, so evaluate retrieval first.

questions.question: How is a Cortex Search Service governed?
options: Anyone with its URL can query it
It is a Snowflake object controlled by the same RBAC as tables
Only Snowflake Support can query it
questions.explanation: Access to Cortex objects is granted to roles like any other Snowflake object.

questions.question: What does a Cortex Agent do with its tools?
options: Runs every tool for every question
Plans the request and picks the right tool or tools, such as Analyst, Search or a custom tool
questions.explanation: Agents orchestrate multi-step work, routing structured questions to Cortex Analyst and document questions to Cortex Search.

questions.question: What is Snowflake Intelligence / CoWork for?
options: A governed, no-code chat experience for business users on top of agents
questions.explanation: It puts agents in front of business users without them writing SQL, under the same governance.

questions.question: Which is a concrete cost-saving move for production?
questions.explanation: Shorter auto-suspend, smaller default warehouses, serverless tasks and tight Resource Monitors all cut idle spend.

questions.question: What does the Trust Center help you do?
options: Review account security posture, such as users without MFA
questions.explanation: Trust Center scans the account against security recommendations and surfaces findings to fix.

questions.question: Before registering for a SnowPro exam, what should you always check?
options: The current official exam guide on snowflake.com
questions.explanation: Exam guides and product names change, so the official guide is the source of truth.
